hints: Count every atom shown in the asparagine skeleton carefully, remembering that each line end or junction is a carbon and adding the hydrogens on the two $\text{NH}_2$ groups and the $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}$ groups.
walkthrough:
Count the backbone carbons**
Look at asparagine from left to right. You have $\text{C}(=\text{O})$ of the side chain amide, then $\text{CH}_2$, then $\text{CH}$, then $\text{C}(=\text{O})$ of the acid. That is 4 carbons in total.

Add up H, N and O**
There are two nitrogens from the two $\text{NH}_2$ groups and three oxygens from the two $\text{C}=\text{O}$ groups plus the $\text{OH}$. Counting hydrogens: $2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 8$ hydrogens. So you get $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$.

hints: Look separately at the left end, the middle bottom, and the right end of asparagine and ask what carbon plus nitrogen or oxygen combination you see in each place.

Remember that $\text{CONH}_2$ is different from $\text{NH}_2$ alone, and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is different from just $\text{C}=\text{O}$, so check for all three nitrogen and oxygen containing groups.
walkthrough:
Spot the three reactive sites**
On the left you have $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{NH}_2$. That carbonyl joined directly to nitrogen is an amide. In the middle bottom you have a simple $\text{NH}_2$ attached to carbon, that is an amine, specifically a primary amine. On the right you have $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{OH}$, that is a carboxylic acid.

Why all three count**
It is easy to think there are just amino and acid groups because it is an amino acid. But asparagine has an extra amide in its side chain $\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$. So the full set is amide, amine and carboxylic acid.
Final answer: amide ($\text{CONH}_2$), amine ($\text{NH}_2$) and carboxylic acid ($\text{CO}_2\text{H}$)

hints: Recall that a dipeptide forms by condensation between the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ of one amino acid and the $\text{NH}_2$ on the alpha carbon of the other, with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Think about which new linkage is created and how it must be drawn displayed as $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{N}(\text{H})$ and clearly labelled as the peptide bond.
walkthrough:
Join acid to amine**
Imagine taking the $\text{OH}$ from the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ of valine and an $\text{H}$ from the alpha $\text{NH}_2$ of asparagine. Those combine to lose $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. What is left joins as $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{N}(\text{H})$. That is your new peptide bond.

Draw the full dipeptide correctly**
Keep both side chains untouched: valine contributes $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ which can be written as $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$, asparagine contributes $\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$. So one valid form is $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7)\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{N}(\text{H})\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Draw the peptide $\text{C}=\text{O}$ and $\text{N}\text{H}$ fully displayed and label that link peptide bond. Joining the other way round to give Asp-Val is equally correct.

Final answer: Val-Asp dipeptide: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7)\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{N}(\text{H})\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ with the $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{N}(\text{H})$ linkage shown displayed and labelled peptide / amide bond. The reverse Asp-Val isomer is also accepted.

hints: Think about what makes a buffer special compared with pure water when you add a drop of acid or alkali, focus on what happens to pH.
Remember the definition must state the amount condition, a buffer does not cope with unlimited acid or alkali, only a particular quantity.
walkthrough:
Picture the key behaviour**
If you add a little $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$ to water, pH swings dramatically. A buffer soaks up that added $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$, so pH stays within a very small range.

Add the small amount condition**
No buffer works for ever. The definition always includes that this resistance applies when only a small amount of acid or base is added. Large additions will overwhelm it.
Final answer: A solution that resists change in pH / keeps pH almost constant when a small amount of acid or alkali is added.

hints: Use the given form $\text{H}_2\text{NCHRCO}_2\text{H}$ and decide which end, the basic $\text{NH}_2$ or the acidic $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, will react with added $\text{H}^+$ and which will react with added $\text{OH}^-$.
Write each as a balanced equation showing proton gain to give $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+$ and proton loss to give $\text{CO}_2^-$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Remove added acid using the amine**
Valine has a basic $\text{NH}_2$ group. When $\text{H}^+$ is added, that lone pair accepts the proton: $$\text{H}_2\text{NCHRCO}_2\text{H} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CHRCO}_2\text{H}$$ This removes free $\text{H}^+$, so pH hardly falls.

Remove added alkali using the acid**
Valine also has an acidic $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group. When $\text{OH}^-$ is added, the acid donates a proton to neutralise it: $$\text{H}_2\text{NCHRCO}_2\text{H} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{NCHRCO}_2^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ This removes free $\text{OH}^-$, so pH hardly rises. Having both acidic and basic groups in one molecule is what makes the amino acid a buffer.

hints: Identify the four different groups on the alpha carbon of valine: $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and R where $\text{R} = (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}$, and recall how a tetrahedral centre is drawn with solid wedge and hashed wedge bonds.
Think about what the second isomer must look like relative to the first to be its mirror image, with two groups swapped in space while keeping all connections the same.
walkthrough:
Set up the chiral centre in 3D**
The alpha carbon is bonded to four different groups: $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{H}$, $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{R}$. Draw the central C with one bond as a solid wedge coming out toward you and one as a hashed wedge going away, plus two normal lines, to show a tetrahedron.

Draw the mirror image pair**
Draw the first enantiomer, for example with $\text{NH}_2$ on a wedge on the left and H on a dash on the right. Then draw the second structure as its exact mirror, swapping left and right so $\text{NH}_2$ and H (or R and H) are reversed. Check that the two cannot be superimposed, they are mirror images with the same four groups but opposite spatial arrangement.

Final answer: Two tetrahedral structures centred on the alpha C bonded to $\text{NH}_2$, H, R and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, drawn with wedge and dash bonds as non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

hints: Look at which amide in asparagine will hydrolyse under hot aqueous acid, the side chain $\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$ rather than the alpha amino acid backbone, and recall that amide plus water gives acid plus ammonia.
Write the equation using condensed formulas for asparagine and the aspartic acid product, adding $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the left and $\text{NH}_3$ on the right and balancing.
walkthrough:
Spot the group that hydrolyses**
Hot aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ hydrolyses amides. In asparagine the vulnerable group is the side chain primary amide $\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$. Hydrolysis means adding water across the $\text{C}\text{N}$ bond: $\text{CONH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_3$.

Write the full equation**
Keep the rest of the molecule unchanged. Asparagine $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ becomes aspartic acid $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H})\text{CO}_2\text{H}$: $$\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2)\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H})\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_3$$ Under strongly acidic conditions this can also be written protonated as $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H})\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_4^+$.
